STA TEMENT OF OBJECTS  AND REASONS
Assisted reproductive technology (ART) has grown by leaps and bounds in the last
few years. India has highest growths in the ART centres and the number of ART cycles
performed every year. Assisted Reproductive Technology including in-vitro-fertilisation,
has given hope to a multitude of persons suffering from infertility, but it has also introduced
a plethora of legal, ethical and social issues.
2. India has over the years become one of the major centres of this global fertility
industry, with reproductive medical tourism becoming a significant activity. Clinics in India
offer nearly all the ART services—gamete donation, intrauterine insemination, in-vitro-
fertilisation, intra cytoplasmic sperm injection, pre-implantation genetic diagonistic and
gestational surrogacy. However, in spite of so much activity in India, there is yet no
standardisation of protocols and reporting is still very inadequate. Furthermore, there is no
law to regulate ART and it is regulated through guidelines.
3.  The need to regulate the Assisted Reproductive Technology Services is mainly to
protect the affected women and children from exploitation. The oocyte donor needs to be
supported by an insurance cover. Multiple embryo implantation needs to be regulated and
children born through ART need to be protected. The cryopreservation of sperm, oocytes
and embryo by the ART Banks need to be regulated and the proposed legislation intends to
make Pre Genetic Implantation Testing mandatory for the benefit of the child born through
assisted reproductive technology.
4. There is a need to regulate ART clinics and banks by establishing the National
Board, the State Boards, the National Registry and the State Registration Authorities for the
regulation and supervision of assisted reproductive technology clinics and the assisted
reproductive technology banks, for prevention of misuse and for safe and ethical practice of
assisted reproductive technology services.
5. The proposed legislation, namely, the Assisted Reproductive Technology
(Regulation) Bill, 2020 proposes to regulate the Assisted Reproductive Technology services
in the country. The salient features of the Bill are as follows:—
(a) to define certain terms like "assisted reproductive technology", "assisted
reproductive technology clinic", "commissioning couple", "Woman", etc.;
(b) to provide that the National Board and the State Board shall be the same
Board as proposed in the Surrogacy Bill;
(c) to provide that the existing assisted reproductive technology clinics and the
assisted reproductive technology banks, as on the date of the enactment of the
proposed legislation, conducting assisted reproductive technology procedures partly
or exclusively shall make an application to the Registration Authority within a period
of sixty days from the date of establishment of the National Registry;
(d) to provide that the assisted reproductive technology services shall be
available to a woman above the legal age of marriage and below the age of fifty years
and a man above the legal age of marriage and below the age of fifty-five years;
(e) to provide that an oocyte donor shall be an ever married woman having at
least one live child of her own with a minimum age of three years and to donate oocytes
only once in her life and not more than seven oocyte shall be retrieved from the oocyte
donor;
(f) to provide that the assisted reproductive technology clinics shall provide
professional counselling to commissioning couple and woman about all the implications
16

17
and chances of success of assisted reproductive technology procedures in the clinic;
and they shall also inform the advantages, disadvantages and cost of the procedures,
their medical side effects, risks including the risk of multiple pregnancy and any such
other matter as may help the commissioning couple to arrive at an informed decision
that would most likely be the best for the commissioning couple and woman;
(g) to provide that the assisted reproductive technology clinics and assisted
reproductive technology banks shall ensure that commissioning couple, woman and
donors of gametes are eligible to avail of assisted reproductive technology procedures;
(h) to provide for offences and penalties for the contravention of its provisions.
6. The Notes on clauses explain in detail the various provisions contained in the Bill.
7. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
 The Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Bill, 2020 has been proposed for
the regulation and supervision of the assisted reproductive technology clinics and the
assisted reproductive technology banks, prevention of misuse, safe and ethical practice of
assisted reproductive technology services. The proposed legislation, is framed in such a
manner that it ensures effective regulation with the creation of the National Board, National
Registry, State Boards and Registration Authorities at the Centre and State / Union-territory
level.
2. Clause 3 of the Bill provides that the National Board to be constituted under
sub-section ( 1) of section 15 of the Surrogacy Act shall be the National Board for the
purposes of the proposed legislation.
3. Clause 6 of the Bill provides that the State Board to be constituted under
sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Surrogacy Act shall be the State Board for the purposes
of the proposed legislation.
4. Clause 9 of the Bill provides that the Central Government may, by notification,
establish for the purposes of the proposed legislation, a Registry to be called the National
Registry of Clinics and Banks in India.
5. Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 12 of the Bill provides that the Central Government shall,
within a period of ninety days from the date of commencement of the proposed legislation,
by notification, appoint one or more Registration Authorities for each of the Union territories
for the purposes of the proposed legislation.
6. Sub-clause ( iii) of clause 4, sub-clause ( iv) of clause 7 and sub-clause ( 4) of
clause 12 of the Bill respectively provides that the members of the National Board, State
Board and Registration Authority, other than ex officio members shall receive only
compensatory travelling expenses for attending the meetings.
7. Clause 10 of the Bill provides that the National Registry referred to in section 9 shall
consist of scientific, technical, administrative and supportive staff.
8. There will not be any financial implications except for the meetings of the National
Board, the State Board, the Registration Authority and the aforesaid staff of the National
Registry which will be met out of the regular budget of the Central Government and the State
Governments.
9. The Bill does not involve any other expenditure of recurring or non-recurring nature
from the Consolidated Fund of India.

security, recording and identification under sub-section (1) of section 28; (w) the manner of
obtaining the consent of the commissioning couple or individual for perishing of the gametes
of a donor or embryo under sub-section (2) of section 28; (x) research on human embryo
under sub-section (2) of section 30; (y) the manner of entry and search by the National
Board, the National Registry or the State Board or any officer authorised by it under
sub-section (1) of section 40.
2.  Clause 43 of the Bill seeks to empower the National Board, with the prior approval
of the Central Government, by notification, to make regulations consistent with the proposed
legislation and the rules made thereunder to provide for-- (a) the manner of harvesting the
oocytes under clause (a) of section 24; (b) the number of oocytes or embryos under
clause (b) of section 24; and (c) any other matter which is required to be, specified by
regulations or in respect of which provision is to  be made by regulations.
3. The matters in respect of which the aforementioned rules and regulations may be
made are matters of procedure and administrative detail, and as such, it is not practicable to
provide for them in the proposed Bill itself. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore,
of a normal character.

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE GOVERNMENT 
IV. NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION  
Recommendations/Observations 
4.3 The Committee notes that NRHM is the most am bitious Project proposed to be launched in the 
Health and Family Welfare Sector. Mission has received the Cabinet approval very recently, i.e. 4th January 
2005. States are being now advised to undertake prep aratory activities. The Committee has been given to 
understand that in view of the recent Cabinet approv al, requirement for activities under NRHM could not 
be included in the proposal sent to the Planning Commission. A minimum of Rs. 600 crores will be 
required as additional budgetary support during 2005-06. 
Action Taken 
 Planning Commission has accorded in principle approval of Rs. 900 crores as additionality for 2005-
06 for National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) at RE stag e subject to availability of funds. The details of 
the scheme-wise allocation of funds of Rs. 900 crores are as under: 
(Rs. in crores) 
Sl. No. Activity Allocation 
1. Upgrading Public Health Infrastructure 400 
2. Mobile Medical Unit 200 
3. Drug Supply 200 
4. Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)/Na tional Maternity Benefit Scheme 60 
5. National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme 40 
 TOTAL : 900 
VI. URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES  
Recommendations/Observations 
6.5 The Committee has taken seriously the underut ilization of funds under Urban Family Welfare 
Services for a number of years in succession and the reason being the same. The Department perhaps did 
not take any remedial steps to improve the si tuation. The Committee feels that based on the 
recommendations of the evaluation study, steps should be taken for strengthening/expansion of the scheme. 
Action Taken 
 During the years 2002-03 and 2003-04, the shortfall was due to 10% statutory provision of total 
budget made for North-Eastern States, whereas their re quirements were very less. As there are no Health 
Posts in NE region, the 10 per cent of the total budget of Urban Health Posts could not be utilized.  
 During 2004-05, the budget allocation for thes e two schemes was Rs. 121.00 crores, which was 
entirely utilized. There is no under utilization of fu nds under these schemes. Wh en the final evaluation 
report is received, requisite action will be taken for strengthening/expanding of the scheme, subject to 
availability of funds. 
VII. REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)  
Recommendations/Observations 
7.3 The Committee would however like to emphasize that besides organizing workshops/meetings with 
State/district level officials, inspections both regular/ surprise by designated Central officials should also be 

initiated. The Committee welcomes all these very significant initiatives being taken by the Department and 
hopes that they would be implemented as envisaged to get the desired results. 
Action Taken 
 With a view to getting the desired results, th e second phase of the RCH programme encourages 
decentralized need based planning by the States. Furthe r, specific attention is being paid by the programme 
to develop the programme management capabilities at th e District and the State levels through induction of 
skilled professionals. A carefully thought out monito ring and evaluation system is expected to provide 
regular feedback on the implementation of the progra mme, using both Departmental as well as community 
based feedback mechanisms. Consiste nt with the directions of the Committee, Nodal Officers have been 
designated to maintain oversight over the implementation of the programme in the States. 
Recommendations/Observations 
7.5  The Committee observes that more or less the sa me factors were responsible for underutilisation in 
the first two years of the Tenth Plan. The Committee notes that an enhanced allocation of Rs. 1380.68 
crores has been made for 2005-06, based upon an assessment of demands of the States/UTs, and the 
committed liabilities of the States. The Committee view s with serious concern the availability of unspent 
funds with different States under this programme. 
Action Taken 
 The Ministry expects improved off take under the programme as a result of decentralized planning, 
programme management capacity building at the State and District levels and introduction of new 
monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. In so far as availability of unspent funds with different States under 
the programme is concerned, the States have been se nsitized on the need to settle releases made upto 
31.3.2005 under the first phase of the programme. A DO letter to all the States/UTs has already been 
written on 24.5.2005. As a result, 5 States have resp onded and reminders to the other States are being 
issued so that the unspent balances lying with them may be refunded/adjusted as early as possible. It is also 
proposed to organize workshops with the States/UTs to settle issues relating to unspent funds. 
Recommendations/Observations 
7.7 The Committee notes that the Department has in itiated some remedial measures, creating State and 
District Management Units, engaging qualified Mana gers, Accounts persons and a qualified Financial 
Expert which are the required initiatives. The propos al of the Govt. to continue with the process of 
organizing workshops and meetings with State and di strict level officers is welcome. The Committee, 
would, however, like to emphasize that besides organizing workshops/meetings with State/district level 
officers, inspections both regular and surprise by designated Central Govt. officials should also be initiated. 
Action Taken 
 As mentioned in response to Para No.7.3, with a view to getting the desired results, the second phase 
of the RCH programme encourages decentralized need  based planning by the States. Further, specific 
attention is being paid by the programme to develop the programme management capabilities at the District 
and the State levels through induction of skilled prof essionals. A carefully th ought out monitoring and 
evaluation system is expected to provide regular fe edback on the implementation of the programme using 
both Departmental as well as community based feedback  mechanisms. Consistent with the directions of the 
Committee, Nodal Officers have been designated to  provide oversight to the implementation of the 
programme in the States/UTs. 
Recommendations/Observations 
7.8 The Committee has some apprehensions about the fe asibility of the new methodology proposed to be 
adopted for release of Central financial assistance und er RCH-II. In view of very poor performance of the 
various State Govts. in majority of the components of  RCH programme so far, the flexibility now proposed 
to be given to them may prove to be counter-producti ve. The Committee is of the view that the Department 
in the initial years will have to play a pro-active role in the formulation and implementation of State 
Specific Plans with an inbuilt effective monitoring m echanism. With the option now being made available 

to the State Govt. to prioritize their schemes as per the local requirements, involvement of public 
representatives, reputed NGOs and Panchayat Raj In stitutions will prove to be very beneficial. The 
Committee, therefore, is of the view that the Department should evolve a system where under besides State 
Govts. other Stakeholders also have a decisive role to play. 
Action Taken 
 In keeping with the suggestions of the Committee, from the very outset the Government of India is 
closely involved with the planning and programme im plementation process under RCH-II. To this end, a 
model National Programme Implementation Plan was deve loped and shared with the States/UTs to enable 
them to formulate their respective pl ans. Thereafter consultations involving all the States/UTs were held to 
assist them in formulating their specific proposals. The States/UTs experiencing difficulties in formulating 
their respective proposals were provided with expert technical assistance for developing their plans. 
Further, clear guidelines on appraisal of State PIPs we re formulated and circulated to the States/UTs in 
advance so as to enable them to fo rmulate appropriate proposals. Finally, a participative process has been 
adopted for evaluation of the State Programme Implementation Plans wherein detailed discussions have 
been held with representatives of each and every State before approving the individual plan. The RCH-II 
also, as suggested by the Committee,  envisages involvement of public representatives, reputed NGOs and 
Panchayati Raj Institutions so as to ensure that the stakeholders have a role to play. 
VIII.  JANANI SURAKSHA YOJANA (NATIONAL MATERNITY BENEFIT  SCHEME) 
Recommendations/Observations 
8.2 The Committee observes that exerci se of revision of this scheme has been going on for the last two 
years. As a result, funds allocated have remained underutilized. Against the allocation of Rs.500 crores in 
the Tenth Plan, the expenditure for first two years is only Rs. 87.57 crores and the balance available for the 
remaining period is Rs.300.43 crores. The Committee feels that there should be no further delay and 
finalization of the schemes should be expedited. The Committee would also like to emphasize that the 
Department should not be complacent by just revi sing the scheme, rather an effective monitoring 
mechanism should be evolved for its proper implementation. 
Recommendations/Observations 
8.3 The Committee has observed that under the existin g scheme, there is no mechanism to ascertain the 
exact number of actual beneficiaries of the scheme . The Department has been estimating the number of 
beneficiaries on the basis of amount of grants released  to the District authorities. The Committee feels that 
under the proposed revised scheme, there should be an i nbuilt mechanism so that there is periodic survey to 
verify the exact number of beneficiaries. The Committee also observes that State-wise details of estimated 
number of beneficiaries indicate that those States wh ere need for population stab ilization measures is the 
most do not seem to be taking benefit of this sche me. The Committee is of the opinion that the revised 
scheme should be given due publicity, specially in backward/tribal areas. 
Recommendations/Observations 
8.4  The Committee has also noticed that under th e existing Scheme due to unspent balances, non 
receipt/late receipt of UCs/Audited accounts/receipt of incomplete/incorrect documents, there was improper 
and underutilization of allocated funds. This was evid ent in respect of all the States in the country. The 
Committee, would therefore, like to em phasize that all preventive measures need to be taken to avoid such 
problems/shortcomings under the revised scheme. 
Action Taken 
 The scheme of Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY ) has been approved by Cabinet Committee of 
Economic Affairs on 29.3.05 and the scheme has come into force w.e.f. 12.4.05. Under the scheme, 
assistance to expectant mother in rural areas is of Rs . 700/-per delivery. In urban areas of low performing 
States, the expectant mother will receive an amount of Rs.600/- per delivery. Moreover, in the Scheme, 

Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) would be  working as link between the poor expectant mothers 
and the health institutions. 
 In the Janani Suraksha Yojana, monitoring and evaluation aspects have been given due thrust. A time 
bound reporting mechanism has been drawn in th e guidelines of the sc heme. The State Health 
Mission/State Implementation Committe es has been given flexibility to institute adequate and appropriate 
arrangements for monitoring and evaluation of the scheme. The Central Government also proposes to 
establish an independent monitoring and evaluation mechanism. 
 Under the guidelines of the scheme, a clear cut reporting mechanism has been drawn up under which 
the State Implementation Committee is mandatorily required to send six-monthly district-wise reports along 
with SOE/UC/ARs in the prescribed format including number of beneficiaries. 
IX.  STRENGTHENING OF IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME AND ERADICATION OF 
POLIO 
Recommendations/Observations 
9.4  The main reason for underutilisation of funds is non-receipt of UCs and unspent balances available 
with the States. On a specific query about the co nstraints being faced by the State Govts. in the 
implementation of this programme, it was clarified that  details of expenditure figures and unspent balances 
from the remote districts were not being received by the State Govts. This resulted in delay in preparation 
of UCs for submission of the Central Govt. The Committee is not inclined to agree with the justification for 
underutilization of funds given by the Department. The Committee feels that the Department will have to 
focus on State-specific strategies for optimum and judicious utilisation of allocated funds. The Committee 
observes that as per RHS-2002, immunization level of ch ildren is 49 per cent. The Department will have to 
make concerted efforts to reach the ta rget of 100 per cent coverage of children under immunization against 
six preventable diseases by the end of Tenth Plan, 2007. 
Action Taken 
 The suggestion of the Committee for focusing on Stat e-specific strategies for optimum and judicious 
utilization of funds is taken note of. It may be mentioned that State specific strategies have been included in 
the recently launched National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Under NRHM, funds will be released to the 
States on the basis of their own Project Implementati on Plans (PIPs). Since fund s will be based on the 
States’ requirements, as reflected in their PIPs, the St ates will be accountable for the physical and financial 
progress in the implementation of the various programmes, including immunization. The Government has 
embarked upon a number of additional supports to the States for facilitating 100% immunization coverage 
of children against six preventable diseases. The add itional supports will be in respect of (i) alternative 
vaccine delivery at immunization sites, (ii) holding  of sessions in slums and under-served areas, (iii) 
mobilization of children by ASHA, etc. to immunizatio n session sites, (iv) mobility support to District 
Immunization Officers, (v) provision of Computer Assistant to the districts, (vi) six-monthly review 
meetings with the districts at Stat e level, and (vii) implementation of State-specific strategies. These 
additional supports are intended to (i) facilitate better and timely service delivery by the ground level staff, 
and (ii) improve the quality of monitoring and superv ision. The performance of the States, especially the 
poor performing States, in the area of pulse polio programme and Routine Immunization programme is 
closely being monitored. 
 The Government of India has also decided to introduce Auto Disable (AD) syringes for 
administering all vaccines (except oral polio vaccine) under Universal Immunization Programme. Besides 
ensuring injection safety, it will also improve the implementation of the programme. Supplies of AD 
syringes are expected to start from August-September, 2005. 
Recommendations/Observations 
9.6 The Committee is a bit apprehensive of the commitm ent of the Government to eradicate all strains of 
the poliovirus in near future. The Department has now confirmed that as on 14
th March 2005, 136 cases of 
Polio were reported in the country in 2004, out of which 82 were from U.P. and that too, 21 from 
Moradabad and 12 from Badaun district. Analysis of  cases in Moradabad and Badaun has shown that poor 

micro-planning, training and social m obilization are the main factors responsible for high rate of Polio in 
these districts. 
Action Taken 
 The Polio eradication programme in India made greater progress in the last three years than ever 
before, with cases dropping from 1600 in 2002 to 134 in 2004, and affected districts falling from 157 in 
2002 to 44 last year. The virus is now confined to its last strongholds in UP and Bihar. However, 
eradication of poliovirus in UP and Bihar requires immunization of all children less than 5 years with 
multiple doses of oral polio vaccine (OPV). 
 The Govt. of India and the State Governments are taking all possible measures to ensure 100 per cent 
coverage of children below 5 years of age. Micro-plans of the high-risk districts of Uttar Pradesh have been 
strengthened so as to ensure that no house/child is missed during polio rounds. 
 Special training module of vacci nators and supervisors engaged in  the conduct of the rounds has 
been developed and these staff has been trained as  per these improved modules. This has resulted in 
improved quality of training and consequent improved activities. 
 Additional personnel have been deployed by the State and district administrations, UNICEF & 
Rotary International for better involvement of the community in the programme. 
Recommendations/Observations 
9.8 Committee’s attention has been drawn by Media reports that Bihar has recorded 41 cases of Polio in 
2004, more than double the number of cases reported in 2003 which stood at 18. The Committee 
understands that these cases are scattered all over  in Bihar with Patna, Khagaria, Madhepura and 
Muzaffarpur being the worse affected. Already two cases have been reported from the State in 2005. On a 
specific query in this regard, the Department conf irmed the media reports about Bihar. The Committee 
finds that the justification given by the Department th at due to poor quality of rounds undertaken between 
July to Sept. 2004 because of floods cannot be cons idered very convincing. Th e Committee feels that the 
Department has to anticipate this kind of situations and take remedial action well in time. The Committee 
hopes that with the high quality of supplementary immunization activity planned for 2005, things would 
improve in the State. The Committee would also like to emphasize that the remedial measures as initiated in 
affected districts of U.P. in the wake of increase in th e number of Polio cases may also be undertaken in all 
the affected districts of Bihar. 
Action Taken 
 The concerns of the Committee have been noted for compliance. 
 For ensuring quality implementation of the rounds during floods, Flood Plans have been prepared for 
all the districts of Bihar. These Plans envisage that people would move in boats to specific places during 
floods where vaccines, vaccinators and other logistics would be reached as per plan. 
 The Government, in collaboration with partners, has taken a number of initiatives in the recent 8 
months to stop poliovirus transmission in high-risk di stricts of UP and Bihar. These include (1) introducing 
vaccine targeting the one type of wild polio virus which is now most common in India (monovalent OPV); 
(2) increasing vaccination teams at high volume transit sites like train and bus stations; (3) coordinating an 
approach to immunizing children on trains with the Railway Ministry; (4) redeployment and concentration 
of WHO, UNICEF and Government personnel with extensive expertise in the highest risk districts; (5) 
revision of micro plans; and (6) intensive investigation of cases to identify how the virus is spreading in the 
last phase of eradication. 
X. JANSANKHYA STHIRTA KOSH  
Recommendations/Observations 
10.3 The Committee expresses its serious concern about the fate of a project initiated with laudable 
objective. It took three years to implement the de cision of setting up the Kosh. Almost two years have 
passed since then and the seed mone y of Rs.100 crores available under  the Kosh is lying unutilized. The 
Committee can understand the total lack of contri butions/donations from an y sector. The Committee, 

however, fails to understand the rationale for non-utilisation of funds available under the Kosh. The 
Committee finds that the approval of th e Cabinet has been obtained for reco nstitution of the Kosh so as to 
increase its membership and establish it as an autonom ous society, free to operate in a non-bureaucratic 
mode. The Committee would like to emphasize that adequate publicity about the availability of funds under 
the Kosh for providing financial as sistance for Projects on Population Stabilisation and also for inviting 
contribution to the same needs to be given. 
Action Taken 
 The Janasankhya Sthirata Kosh (JSK) was established as an autonomous body, registered under the 
Societies Registration Act on 12th June, 2003 with a view to provide a window for canalising resources 
through voluntary contributions from individuals, in dustry, trade organisations and others, and support 
projects, schemes, initiatives and innovative ideas designed to achieve population stabilisation at a level 
consistent with the socio-economic development of the country. Government has contributed a sum of 
Rs.100 crores towards the corpus of the Fund. 
 It has to be appreciated that the Department of  Health & Family Welfare is managing a budgetary 
allocation in the range of Rs.5000 crores every year, of which the Budget for NGO Division and private 
sector by way of Social Franchise, Mother NGO Scheme etc. is already in the range of more than Rs.100 
crores per annum. Thus the utili zation of the income of the Kosh did not present any administrative 
challenge to the Department, rather the Department  insisted on adopting the unorthodox approach of 
ensuring a non-bureaucratic mode for operationalization of the Kosh and utilization of its income. Due to 
less than encouraging response of NGOs and corporate sector, and the need for a renewed Cabinet 
revalidation, this has taken some time. However,  the Department is committed to reconstitution, 
energization and full operationalizati on of the Kosh in the current year. As per the Cabinet approval, the 
corpus of Rs.100 crores shall be deposited in a Ba nk Account or Government Securities. The earnings of 
the Kosh by way of interest earned on the corpus, do nations from individuals, industry, trade organisations

th June 2005. Now the scope for membership

1.5 Committee is not fully convinced by the contention of the Department that SRS, RGI have estimated 
the MMR for the country as 407 per 100,000 live births in 1998 which is the same period when NFHS-II 
have estimated the MMR as 540 per 100,000 live births. The fact remains that there are some problem areas 
in data collection. No availability of reliable estimates of maternal mortality has been admitted by the 
Department also in its Annual Report (2004-05). The Committee notes that an expert group has been 
constituted in the Department which is looking into the modalities of carrying out a survey for collection of 
data on maternal mortality. A pilot survey for this ha s already been completed. Similar problems may be 
there in respect of other health indicators also. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the Department 
should carry out a comparative analysis of findings of NFHS-I and NFHS-II in order to understand the 
factors responsible for discrepancies in the two Survey Reports. The Committee would also like to 
emphasize that the entire Family Welfare planning is based on the National Surveys being conducted at 
regular intervals. Therefore, it should be ensured that accurate data is ma de the basis of all health surveys. 
This can be achieved to a large extent by monitoring of data being obtained specially from the States not 
performing well by involving Central teams also in the collection of data, to the extent possible.

 NFHS-I & II estimates are widely accepted at al l levels both in the country and internationally 
among policy makers. Reason for wide variation in MMR estimated from SRS and NFHS is large sampling

that despite routine performance reports sent by State/UT Governments, the Ministry also undertake 
evaluation surveys through independent professional agencies in the field of health and family welfare 
sector. Besides, there are regional evaluation teams located in the offi ces of Regional Directors, who 
undertake regular sample ve rification of health care delivery system and various records maintained by 
ANMs. At present there are seven Regional Evaluation  Teams (RETs) located at Delhi, Lucknow, Patna, 
Bangalore, Chennai, Bhopal and Kolkata functioning for sample verification of fa mily welfare acceptors,

Recommendations/Observations 
3.3 The Committee is not hopeful about full utili zation of allocated funds in 2004-05. The Committee 
expresses its serious concern over the element of unspe nt balances available under majority of the schemes 
during the first three years of the Tenth Plan. The very fact that unspent balances continue to be available 
from year to year under any scheme can lead to only two conclusions. Either the projected allocation has 
not been based on a scientific assessment or failure of  the implementing agencies  in reaching the targeted 
beneficiaries. Both the situations  need serious review/rethinking of implementation process of such 
schemes. The Committee would, accordingly, impress up on the Department to take remedial measures in 
the matter. 
Action Taken 
 The unspent balance available with the State Governments underline the need for better ownership of 
programmes for which funds are released by the Government of India and for professional management and 
accounting of funds. Under the paradigm adopted under NRHM/RCH-II, financial envelopes have been 
conveyed to State Governments within which they can plan the activities for attainment of goals. It is hoped 
that such decentralization of pla nning and management of funds woul d result in increased ownership of 
programmes at State level. 
 The expected outlay of the State for Health and Family Welfare has been conveyed in April 2005 to 
ensure predictability of funds and enable better plan ning for the same. Up to 6 per cent funds under RCH 
State Programme Implementation Plans are being provided towards management cost. In EAG States, the 
Government of India has assisted in creation of State and District Programme Management Unit through 
contractual engagement of skilled professionals like MBA, CA, MIS Specialist etc. The States have also 
been assisted in the process of recruiting manpower for such posts. Additionally, the system of e-banking is 
proposed to be piloted in six States for improved tracking and accountability of funds. Nodal Officers in the 
rank of Joint Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India have been 
identified for the States to oversee and guide in better implementation of programmes. It is hoped that these 
remedial measures will lead to better utilization of funds. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee notes that a number of measures have been initiated by the Department under 
NRHM for elimination of unspent balances lying with different states. Th e Committee appreciates 
the streamlining of existing accounting  procedure. The Committee hopes that with the nodal officers 
in place things would improve and result in both better utilization of funds and implementation of 
schemes. 
Recommendations/Observations 
4.4 Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are very much required in th e present scenario. The 
Committee observes that divergent activities not only of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, but 
also number of other Ministries are proposed to be implemented in an integrated manner. Two Departments 
of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare have been integrated for optimum utilisation of financial 
resources and manpower. The Committee, however, has a word of caution in this regard. Both the 
Departments as separate entities were already impl ementing large number of schemes and supervising 
institutions falling under their respective jurisdiction. Not only this, quite a few programmes under both the 
Departments were not being administered effectively due to a very weak monitoring mechanism relying 
only on state figures. The Committee feels that with th e convergence of a number of Health and Family 
Welfare schemes under NRHM, effective monitoring may not be feasible. The Committee, would, 

therefore, emphasize that dilution of services at present available separately under the two Departments 
must be avoided at all costs. 
Action Taken 
 The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) has been constituted with the objective of providing 
comprehensive healthcare facilities for the entire co untry with special focus on 18 States with weak 
demographic indicators and infrastructure, through Public Health Infrastructure by upgrading the same to 
the Indian Public Health Standard (IPHS) and also to provide Health Management Samiti in CHCs/District 
Hospitals to ensure quality services and transparency. 
 The aim of the Mission is to undertake architectural  correction of the Health  System, to enable it to 
effectively handle increased allocations as promis ed under the NCMP. The decentralization of the 
programme to district levels woul d provide greater opportunities for in tersectorality, enabling effective 
utilization of resources through integration and convergence. The District level planning would help 
mobilize large number of stakeholders for improving Public Health facilities at the grass root level. Further, 
the Mission aims at bridging gaps in rural healthcare provisioning by creating a provider in each village and 
providing improved hospital care. Overall, the Mission aims at providing accessible,  affordable, effective, 
accountable and reliable health care to all citizens and in  particular, to the poorer and vulnerable sections of 
the population. 
 To achieve these objectives, it was decided to  merge some of the ongoing programmes of the 
Department of Health & Family Welfare in the States  to have better monitoring, utilization of funds and 
better service providing. The c onvergence of Health and Family Welfare Programmes under NRHM will 
bring consolidated efforts in the Health care servi ce facilities with larger coordination. New posts of 
Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary and Director have been created for the Mission. An officer of the rank 
of Additional Secretary has been appointed as the Mission Director. This would enable proper coordination 
among the programmes subsumed under NRHM within the Department of Health & Family Welfare. Such 
convergence of the two departments was much needed  to rationalize and optimize funds, manpower, MIS, 
training and BCC strategies under the different programmes of HFW. However, the observations of the 
Committee have been noted for compliance. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee finds that to achieve better results under NRHM, some of the ongoing 
programmes of the Department of Health & Family  Welfare in the States have been merged. The 
main idea behind such a move is to have better monitoring, utilization of funds and better service 
providing. New posts have been created. The Committee, however, reiterates its earlier observation 
made in this regard. An effectiv e monitoring mechanism with an in built system of having required 
follow up action should be the most crucial comp onent under NRHM. This is all the more required 
due to convergence of the two Departments. 
V. RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES 
Recommendations/Observations 
5.6 The Committee would like to be apprised of ex act number of Sub-Centres established (State-wise) 
during the, first three years of Tenth Plan. 
Action Taken 
 As per 1991 population, the shortfall in the number of Sub-Centres was to the tune of 8669. Out of 
these 8669, targets were given to 15 States/UTs. Ag ainst these targets, as per the latest information 
available, a total of 2909 Sub-Centres have been established in eight States namely, Haryana, Maharashtra, 
Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttaranchal, West Bengal and Dadra & Nagar Haveli. The State-wise 
position of these Sub-Centres is at Annexure-I. 
Comments of the Committee 

 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the dismal achievement made by majority of 
States in establishing new Sub-centres during the Tenth Plan. Against a target of 8669 Sub-centres, 
only 2909 Sub-centres could be set up so far. Raja sthan, Nagaland, Punjab and West Bengal are the 
only States which have succeeded in achieving their targets. In contrast, in respect of States like 
Bihar and Chhattisgarh, details of Sub-centres set up are not available with the Government 
although fourth year of the Tenth Plan is nearing its end. Similarly, Meghalaya, Orissa, Tripura, U.P. 
and Delhi have failed to set up even a single Sub- centre. Same is the status  of Maharastra which has 
taken almost four years to set up only two Su b-centres against a target of 808 Sub-centres. The 
Committee fails to comprehend the constraints faced by these States in spite of Central assistance 
available for setting up of Sub-centres, at a hi gher level for EAG and NE  States. The Committee 
hopes that under the National Rural Health Mission, all such crucial aspects will be fully taken care 
of. 
Recommendations/Observations 
5.8 The Committee is surprised to note that some St ates have already established PHCs in excess of the 
prescribed norms. There are also States where shortf all in the number of PHCs is evident. Against a 
population norm of 30,000 per PHC, average rural population (2001) per PHC is 45,095 in Bihar, 37,169 in 
Madhya Pradesh, 36,348 in Tripura, 36,169 in U.P., 49,231 in West Bengal and 1,18,090 in Delhi. The 
Committee is not convin ced by the clarifications of the Departme nt that the target for establishment of 
PHCs is given by the Planning Commission to the respec tive States/UTs and it is the responsibility of the 
States/UTs to establish them. The Committee strongly feels that with funds provided under PMGY scheme, 
it is the responsibility of the Department to monitor the establishment of PHCs. 
Action Taken 
 The Planning Commission fixes the targets for the establishment of new Sub-centres/ PHCs/CHCs 
and provides funds for this purpose in the States’ A nnual Health Sector Plans under Primary health care. 
The achievement of these targets is monitored in the Working Group on Health under the Chairmanship of 
Principal Adviser (Health), Planning Commission while discussing the States’ annual health sector plan 
proposals. The Commission, while discussing the Health Plans of the States, also earmarks the funds under 
PMGY. As per the guidelines issued by the Planning Commission, the funds under PMGY are to be utilized 
for procurement of consumables such as reagents, X-ray films, repair of equipments, etc. and for repair, 
maintenance of infrastructure at PHCs/CHCs (water su pply, adequate toilet faci lities, hospital infection 
control and waste management). PMGY funds are not to be utilized for establishment of new infrastructure. 
The Commission also monitors the utilization of funds under PMGY. The Department of FW provides 
funds for strengthening the infrastructural facilities at PHCs/CHCs under the Schemes RCH Flexible Pool, 
and Procurement of Drugs and Equipments. 
 As per the 2001 population norm, 4436 PHCs are ne eded to be established in the country as on 
September, 2004. The State-wise position in respect of PHCs is at Annexure-II. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee observes that as on Septemb er, 2004 (as per 2001 population), there is a 
shortfall of 4436 PHCs spread over in different St ates in the country. The Committee would like to 
point out that the overall figures reveal very dist urbing trends. States like Arunachal Pradesh, 
Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Karnataka, Kerala, Mani pur, Mizoram, Orissa, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil 
Nadu, A&N Islands and Pondicherry have excess number of PHCs. In contrast, States like Bihar, UP 
and West Bengal are yet to establish a large numbe r of PHCs. Such a situation clearly indicates that 
norms for setting up of PHCs are not being strictly  adhered to by the States. In spite of Central 
assistance being provided both fo r establishment of PHCs and provisions of required infrastructure 
and maintenance some States seem to  have failed to take benefit of such assistance. The Department 
should make concerted efforts in getting the required PHCs established in States. 
 The Committee also strongly f eels that there is a need for review of the scheme of health 
centres in rural areas, by having a more flexible approach. 

Recommendations/Observations 
5.9 The Committee finds that the same problem is th ere with regard to CHCs also. Arunachal Pradesh, 
U.P., Mizoram, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and Pondicherry have excess infrastructure in 
terms of CHCs. Capital cost of one CHC is Rs. 80.50 lakhs with a recurr ing liability of Rs. 27.00 lakhs is 
met by the State Governments. under the PMGY progr amme. The Committee is of the opinion that in view 
of the non-adherence to the prescribed population norms , whether short or excess by majority of the States, 
it is time that a review of the existing population norms are looked into by the Department. 
Action Taken 
 As per 2001 population norm, 3332 more CHCs are needed to be established in the Country as on 
September 2004. The State-wise position in respect of CHCs is at Annexure-III. 
 Regarding review of existing population norms,  the issue will be taken up with the Planning 
Commission which had fixed these norms during the Sixth Plan. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee views with seriou s concern the low achievement level of setting up of CHCs in 
different States in the country. The Committee has been  informed that the issue of review of existing 
population norms will be taken up with the Plan ning Commission. The Co mmittee would emphasize 
that the Department should pursue this matter with the Planning Commission so that population 
norms for setting up of CHCs are revised without any further delay. The Committee is disturbed by 
the fact that even those States whose track record about setting up of Sub-centres and PHCs has been 
very good, even having excess number of Centres, ha ve shown a dismal performance level of setting 
up CHCs. The very purpose of having the required /excess number of Sub-centres and PHCs gets 
defeated if the required number of CHCs are not th ere to take care of referral cases from smaller 
centres. 
Recommendations/Observations 
5.11 The Committee understands that the Report of the NCAER study is at present under the 
consideration of the Department. The Committee woul d like to emphasize that the Department should 
initiate action at the earliest for strengthening the f unctioning of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs, the only 
service providers to the targeted beneficiaries in th e remote and inaccessible areas in the country. A 
beginning can be made with the fourteen states where the sample study was conducted by NCAER. The 
Committee would also like to emphasize that a similar st udy is also required to be undertaken with regard 
to the functionaries of both PHCs and CHCs which are also the main service providers like Sub-Centres. 
Action Taken 
 The State-wise Reports presented by NCAER on “Evaluation of functioning of Sub-centres” are 
being forwarded to concerned States for taking appropriate action on the same. 
 Under National Rural Health Missi on, the Sub-centres are proposed to be strengthened by providing 
untied funds for local action @ Rs. 10,000 per annum, supply of essential drugs, both Allopathic and 
AYUSH, to the Sub-centres. Mission is to strengthen  PHCs for quality preventive, promotive, curative, 
supervisory and outreach services th rough adequate and regular supply  of essential quality drugs and 
equipments to PHCs, provision of 24 hours service in at least 50 per cent PHCs by addressing shortage of 
doctors, especially in high focus States, through mainstreaming AYUSH manpower, observance of 
Standard treatment guidelines and protocols. A key strategy of the Mission is operationalising 3222 existing 
CHCs (30-50 beds) as 24 hours First Referral Units, in cluding posting of anesthetists. It also proposes to 
codify new Indian Public Health Standards, promotion of Stakeholder Committees for hospital 
management, developing standards of services and co sts in hospital care and developing, displaying and 
ensuring compliance to Citizens Charter at CHC/PHC leve l. Similar studies, like the study undertaken for 
Sub-Centres, are also being planned for PHCs and CHCs. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee had drawn the attention of th e Department towards the findings of an 
evaluation study of 1040 Sub-Centres covering 300 districts of 14 major states conducted by NCAER 

submitted on the 22nd November, 2004. The Committee is surprised to note that even after one year of 
submission of evaluation study recommendations, the same are still in the process of being forwarded 
to the concerned states. The Committee emphasizes that the Department should pursue with the 
State Govts. the required follow-up action in the light of NCAER evaluation study without any 
further delay. There is an urgent need for conducting similar evaluation studies of PHCs and CHCs 
at the earliest, specially in view of the fact th at National Rural Health Mission has already been 
launched. 
Recommendations/Observations 
5.12 The Committee would like to point out that demo graphically weak states have higher birth rate and 
Infant Mortality Rate. The workload of ANMs in thes e states is thus higher. The Committee, therefore, 
feels that in such states, sanction ing of ANMs should be based on existing norms as per 2001 population. 
At the same time, the Department should also closely monitor the filling up of all the sanctioned posts of 
ANMs. 
Action Taken 
 As on September 2004, the number of ANMs in position in the Country is 138,906 against the 
sanctioned posts of 146,852. The statement indicating State-wise position of ANMs, both sanctioned and in 
position, is at Annexure-IV. 
 RCH Programme, additional ANMs on contractua l basis are provided to the States, wherever 
needed. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee views with serious concern th e shortfall of 11,191 posts of ANMs in the 
country. ANM is an important functionary in Health Care delivery system at local level and therefore 
such a high shortfall of ANMs will adversely affect the system of health care in rural and inaccessible 
areas. The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for non-availability of records regarding 
ANMs in the case of Bihar and Jharkhand. The Committee would like to know about the criteria for 
release of Central Funds for salary of ANMs to states. 
 The Committee recommends that the matter of sh ortfall in the posts of ANMs both which have 
not yet been sanctioned and also sanctioned posts yet to be filled up should be taken up with the 
concerned State Govts. so that work in demographica lly weaker states as well as in the other states 
progresses at a faster pace.

Recommendations/Observations 
7.11 A comparative analysis of funds released a nd achievement level of physical targets of these 
interventions present a very discouraging position. Ag ainst an allocation of Rs. 109.88 crores under ANM 
scheme, only 6335 ANMs were given contractual appointm ent. Similarly, for PHN/Staff Nurse, against an 
allocation of Rs. 31.04 crores, only 1467 PHNs could be given contractual appointment. Allocation for Lab 
Technicians stands at Rs. 8.37 crores, number of cont ractual Lab Technician is only 381. Similarly, for 

hiring of SM consultant, against an allocation of Rs . 3.61 crores, only 1054 Consultants were appointed. 
For hiring of private Anaesthetists, Rs.83.73 lakhs have been provided and number of Anaesthetists hired is 
only 1059. In a number of interventions, although  funds have been duly re leased not even a single 
contractual appointment seems to have been made in th e States of Bihar, Jharkhand, Tripura, Uttaranchal, 
Karnataka. In the case of other States also, level of physical achievement is very poor when compared with 
the quantum of funds released. 
Recommendations/Observations 
7.12 Non-availability of sufficiently qualified manpower in the states is the main reason cited for non-
achievement of contractual appointments of ANMs/PHNs/SNs/Lab Technicians. Sufficient number of 
Anaesthetists in the private sector is  not available at sub-district level. Honorarium of Rs. 800/- per visit 
was not found adequate enough to motivate Safe Motherhood Consultants being mainly lady doctors to 
travel to remote areas. The Committee feels that all th ese interventions that would continue to be available 
under the flexible RCH pool will have  to be revamped in view of th e ground realities. Not only this, 
practice of funds being released without showing any achievement needs a review in view of non-
utilization of such Govt. funds for considerable period. 
Action Taken 
 Under RCH-I, for contractual ap pointments of Addl. ANMs, PHNs/SNs and Lab Technicians, grants 
have been released to the States/UTs on a yearly basis for a specified number of staff worked out as per the 
RCH guideline. As such, the States can make appointmen t every year only within the limit prescribed by 
the Govt. of India and this is the reason for showing fixed number of appointments although the fund 
released has been indicated on the cumulative basis since the inception of Programme. 
 The non-availability of sufficie nt numbers of Anaesthetists and Gynaecologists in most of the 
States/UTs is major hindrance in the smooth implementation of the two schemes. Under RCH-II, most of 
the States, in their Project Implementation Plans (PIPs) , have proposed to implement the schemes either by 
conducting a short training programme for the MBBS doctors or by paying fixed honorarium on a monthly 
basis. 
Comments of the Committee 
 Committee’s attention has been drawn by a number of interventions like cont ractual appointment of 
ANMs, Public Health/Staff Nurse/Lab Technicians an d hiring of Private Anesthetists/ Gynaecologists 
under RCH phase-I. The Committee had commented abou t low level of such appointments by different 
states in spite of considerable central funds being released therefor. The Committee has now been given to 
understand that whereas details of appo intments have been on yearly basi s, details of funds released were 
on cumulative basis. The Committee is not happ y with the kind of information submitted by the 
Department which has resulted in confusion. The Comm ittee would like to be apprised about the details of 
funds released and appointments made under the interv entions of RCH phase-I for the first three years of 
Tenth Plan (year wise). The Committee would also like to point out that amount of honorarium/contractual 
salary for different categories also needs to be reviewed so as to attract the required medical personnel. 
XV. ANNUAL REVIEW REPORTS OF THE DEPARTMENT FOR 2003-04  
Recommendations/Observations 
15.2  The Committee views with serious concern the irregularities in Annual Review Report 2003-04 of 
the Department. The Committee strongly feels that irre gular charging of States’ General side Expenditure 
to the Family Welfare Budget is a very disturbing trend as it has been happening for years. As per the 
information made available to the Committee, amount transferred to Personal Deposit Account is Rs. 1.25 
crores and amount involved due to irregular charging  of States’ General side Expenditure is Rs. 24.50 
crores and the States involved are U.P., Punjab, Haryana, Uttaranchal and UT of Chandigarh. The 
Committee is of the view that the Department shoul d pursue with the concer ned States for corrective 
measures so as to avoid occurrence of such irregularities in future. 

Action Taken 
 The Central Internal Audit Party (CIAP), after doin g the inspection, sends its report to the concerned 
States/UTs with the details of irregularities observed and requests the States/UTs for its compliance so as to 
avoid its recurrence in future. Howe ver, the States/UTs do not respond in the matter and no compliance 
report is received. The Department  has viewed it seriously and the matter is being taken up with the 
concerned States/UTs for its compliance. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee takes serious note about lack of re sponse from States/UTs regarding the inspection 
report of the Central Internal Audit Party (CIAP) mentioning irregularities observed by it. The Committee 
believes such a practice continues because of impr oper accountability measures currently in vogue. The 
Committee is of the view that in such cases, the Department should pursue at the highest level. The 
Committee feels that the Department should devise ad equate measures to increase the accountability of 
states in the wake of which defaulting States/UTs could be asked for compliance.

VII. REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)  
COMMENT OF THE COMMITTEE 
 The Committee takes note of number of in itiatives being taken by the Department for 
elimination of unspent balances with the States an d procurement of utilization certificates from the 
concerned State Govts. The Committee is, however,  not convinced by the proposed method of the 
Department of obtaining refund/adjusting unspent balances against the subsequent withdrawal. Such 
a move will be directly against the set goals, thus defeating the very objectives of the programme. 
Desired action would be to motivate the states to utilize the allocated funds as per the Action Plan. 
  (Para 7.6) 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 Committee’s attention has been drawn by a number of interventions like contractual 
appointment of ANMs, Public Health/Staff Nurse/Lab Technicians and hiring of Private Anesthetists 
Gynaecologists under RCH phase-I. The Committ ee had commented about low level of such 
appointments by different states in spite of cons iderable central funds being released therefor. The 
Committee has now been given to understand that whereas details of appointments have been on 
yearly basis, details of funds released were on cumulative basis. The Committee is not happy with the 
kind of information submitted by the Department which has resulted in confusion. The Committee 
would like to be apprised about the details of funds released and appointments made under the 
interventions of RCH phase-I for the first three years of Tenth Plan (year wise). The Committee 
would also like to point out that amount of hono rarium/contractual salary for different categories 
also needs to be reviewed so as to attract the required medical personnel. (Para 7.11 & 7.12) 
XV. ANNUAL REVIEW REPORTS OF THE DEPARTMENT FOR 2003-04  

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 The Committee takes serious note about lack of response from States/UTs regarding the 
inspection report of the Central Internal Audit Pa rty (CIAP) mentioning irre gularities observed by 
it. The Committee believes such a practice contin ues because of improper accountability measures 
currently in vogue. The Committee is of the view that in such cases, the Department should pursue at 
the highest level. The Committee feels that the Department should devise adequate measures to 
increase the accountability of states in the wake of which defaulting States/UTs could be asked for 
compliance. (Para 15.2)

CHAPTER - I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
ADNIMINISTRATIVE MANAGEMENT OF LOCKDOWN & UNLOCKING  
Observation/Recommendation 
1.1 The Committee is of the view that if we had not hit the history books for guidance, the 
reality would have hit us harder. The Government of India learnt from its experience and took 
successful measures like Janta curfew, imposition of 4 months long lockdown and its gradual 
opening, travel restrictions and other social distancing measures to contain the spread of 
Corona virus. The Committee appreciates the measures but also ob serves that there have been 
few glaring lapses in the battle against pandemic like shortage of emergency supplies, red -
tapism, shortage and quality of testing kits, delay in domestic production etc. 
                        (Para 1.42) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Noted. Yes, in the initial phase of the pandemic, there were issues with the indigenous 
capacity in terms of personal protective equipment, N -95 masks, testing kits, ventilators. 
Government of India rose to the occasion and ensured that the local demand fo r the same is met 
through indigenous production as there was global scarcity for all these items.  
1.3 To fast -track informed decision making and to cut down on the procedural delays, 11 
High level Empowered Groups were formed. Based on the evolving needs and scenario in the 
country, on 11th September 2020, these groups were condensed into six larger empowered 
groups (EGs). Four of the EGs are headed by the departmental secretaries and one each by NITI 
Aayog officials. Each EG is tasked with respective func tions: (i) medical infrastructure and 
COVID management plan, (ii) ensuring availability of essential medical equipment and 
augmenting human resources., disease surveillance and testing, (iii) coordinating with the private 
sector, NGOs and international org anizations for response -related activities, (iv) economic and 
welfare measures, (v) information, communication, public awareness, public grievances and data 
management, (vi) strategic issues related to COVID management, and facilitating supply chain 
and lo gistics management. On 8 th January 2021, another Empowered Group on Vaccine 
Administration has been constituted to take all necessary measures for effective implementation 
of CO-WIN platform created for inventory management and delivery of COVID-19 vaccine. 
CONTINGENCY PLAN 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.4 The Committee is of the view that the unprecedented outbreak of Corona  virus required a 
well-planned and coordinated response from the Central as well as State Governments for 
successful containment of the pandemic. There must be an integrated as well as a decentralized 
response to outbreak of pandemic Covid -19 for rescuing t he common masses. The disease trend 
data under IDSP is crucial for generating the required response to contain the outbreak 

3 
 
especially when Inter Sectoral Coordination for zoonotic diseases is one of the main programme 
components of IDSP. The Committee is constrained to observe the failure of National Centre for 
Disease Control -Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (NCDC -IDSP) in generating the 
required response in the wake of the pandemic. The Committee feels that NCDP -IDSP should 
have been utilized in  a more effective manner especially when the sole objective of IDSP is to 
detect and respond to outbreaks in the early rising phase through trained Rapid Response Teams 
(RRTs). The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for revitalizing the enshrined ro le and 
responsibility of NCDC for effective control of the disease along with strengthening of the 
Central Surveillance Unit (CSU), State Surveillance Units (SSU) and District Surveillance Units 
(DSU). The Committee also recommends the Ministry to effectiv ely implement the various 
programme components under IDSP. The Committee would like the Ministry to launch 
Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme in the remaining States i.e. beyond existing 9 States. 
The Committee observes that there is an urgent need to assess the financial requirement for 
NCDP-IDSP for its revitalization.  
1.5 The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends the Ministry to chalk out 
strategy and specific course of action to revamp the institutional and Human Resource 
Management structure and further strengthen NCDP -IDSP and pursue with the Ministry of 
Finance for higher budgetary allocation to NCDP-IDSP.  
                                      (Para 2.20) 
Action Taken 
 
1.6 In 2015 Joint Monitoring Mission report of Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme 
(IDSP) recommended review and redesign the IDSP surveillance system, including re -
prioritization of the list of diseases under the IDSP. Subsequently, IDSP, NCDC, re -prioritized 
33 priority health conditions for surveillance. 
1.7 Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) is designed & developed by WHO and 
MoHFW in order to have real time data reported under IDSP and different National Health 
Programmes. It is a web -enabled, near -real-time electronic health information syst em that is 
embedded with all applicable  Government of India's e -Governance standards, Information 
Technology (IT), data &meta data standards to provide state -of-the-art single operating picture 
with geospatial information. 
1.8 IHIP implemented currently in 9 States and has now been expanded to all States in April, 
2021. The IHIP is being aligned with the vision document 2035 and roadmap for public health 
surveillance of NITI Aayog. 
1.9 Under the Atmanirbhar Swasth Bharat, the following interventions at an e stimated outlay 
of Rs. 3060 Crores have been made to strengthen NCDC and public health surveillance & 
response: 
 Strengthening of the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), its 5 regional 
branches and 20 metropolitan health surveillance units 
 Setting up integrated public health labs in all districts and 3382 block public health units 
in 11 States 
 Expansion of the Integrated Health Information Portal to all States/UTs to connect all 
public health labs.  

4 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.10 The Committee believes that contact tracing, testing and isolating are the crucial 
components for Covid -19 containment strategy. The Committee is of the view that poor contact 
tracing and slow testing in the initial phase of pandemic led to the increased number of 
infections in the country. 
                                      (Para 2.26) 
Action Taken 
 
1.11 Noted. During VC‟s, through formal communications and deployment of multi -
disciplinary Central teams, States have been repeatedly advised to increase efforts on contact 
tracing with the target to track, trace and test 30 contacts per confirmed case to stop the chain of 
disease transmission in the country. 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.12 The Committee observes that the Pradhan Mantri Atma Nirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojana is 
an ambitious program of the government that encompasses vital components to consolidate and 
enrich health infrastructure in the country. The Committee recommends that government should 
not leave any stone unturned in implementing its every component to achieve its cherished goal. 
                                     (Para 2.29) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13 Recommendations of the Committee have been noted. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.14 The Committee observes that the total number of Government hospital beds in the  
country was grossly inadequate keeping in view the rising incidence of Covid-19 cases. Attention 
of the Committee has also been brought to Media Reports which highlighted the abysmally low 
number of beds in Government hospitals in the country especially a t the peak of the pandemic. 
Data from National Health Profile –2019 states that there are total 7,13,986 Government 
hospital beds available in India which amounts to 0.55 beds per 1,000 population. As per 
Reports, 12 States stand below the national level fi gure. The Committee notes that lack of 
hospital beds and the inadequate ventilators further complicated the efficacy of the containment 
plan against the pandemic. As the numbers of cases were on the rise, a frantic search for vacant 
hospital beds became qu ite harrowing. Instances of patients being turned away from 
overburdened hospitals due to lack of vacant beds became the new normal. The scenario of 
patients holding oxygen cylinder rushing from pillar to post in search of bed in AIIMS Patna is a 
testimony to fact that tear apart humanity. The Committee is aggrieved at the poor state of 
healthcare system and therefore, recommends the Government to increase the investment in 
public health and take appropriate steps to decentralize the healthcare services/fac ilities in the 
country. 
                             (Para 2.34) 
 

5 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.15 The Committee is pained to observe that in RML hospital out of the 1572 beds, only 242 
beds were dedicated COVID beds whereas in Safdarjung Hospital, out of 2 873 beds, only 289 
were reserved for Covid patients. The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind the 
miniscule number of beds reserved for Covid patients in the Central Government Hospitals 
especially at a time when the number of Covid patients was increasing rapidly in the capital city. 
The Committee, therefore, desires the Ministry to submit a note on the rationale for allocating 
such limited number of beds for COVID patients. The Committee would like to be apprised 
regarding the status of beds  exclusively reserved for COVID patients in the capital of the 
country. 
                             (Para 2.35) 
Action Taken 
1.16 Recommendation of the Committee to increase the investment in public health system is 
acknowledged and agreed upon. In this regard, it is submitted that under National Health 
Mission, support is provided to the States/UTs to strengthen their public healthcare system duly 
adopting a health system approach and as NHM targets to build a network for public health 
facilities with He alth & Wellness Centres at the grassroot level and District Hospitals, with

Observation/Recommendation 
1.28 The Committee takes note of the different initiatives taken by ICMR for devising 
treatment protocol for Covid-19. However, the Committee observes that in the initial phase there 
was certain ambiguity in the treatment protocol for Covid -19 which is somehow attributed to the 
mutating strain of Corona virus. The Committee understands that devising a full proof treatment 
plan will have to be substantiated by different p hases of clinical trials and have to be governed 

9 
 
by strict protocols. The Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to widen the scope of its 
clinical research and studies and keep on updating its database which could prove beneficial in 
containing and mitigat ing Covid -19 as well as such future outbreaks. The Committee also 
recommends ICMR to collaborate with other international institutes and pharmaceutical 
companies to test the safety and effectiveness of different drugs and devices. 
                             (Para 3.5) 
Action Taken 
1.29 The COVID-19 Clinical Management Protocol was prepared by MoHFW in consultation 
with AIIMS, New Delhi; National Task Force under ICMR and the Joint Monitoring Group 
under Directorate General of Heal th Services. Last updated algorithm for clinical management 
protocol was issued on 23.04.2021. Similarly, a protocol for Management of Covid - 19 in the 
pediatric Age Group was issued by MoHFW on 29.04.2021. 
 ICMR conducted the world‟s largest clinical tria l on benefit of using plasma therapy in 
COVID-19 infected patients (PLACID Trial). The trial indicated no significant benefit of 
plasma therapy. Thereafter ICMR has issued an advisory in November 2020 regarding use of 
convalescent plasma in COVID-19 infected patients. 
 ICMR has collaborated with Biological Evans to evaluate the efficacy of the hyper -immune 
horse serum for treating COVID -19 infected patients. Similar studies are underway for 
similar product of Serum Institute of India. 
 Collaborations with man ufacturers like ZydusCadila for evaluating monoclonal antibodies 
for treating COVID-19 are also underway. 
 International partnerships were undertaken in the form of WHO Solidarity Trial. Other 
International collaborations are also underway. 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.30 The Committee is of the view that only those drugs whose efficacy for treating COVID -19 
patients have been established should be used for hospitalized patients and the drugs should be 
prescribed only after multicentric trials and detailed study. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to issue clear guidelines for safe use of drugs. The Committee notes 
that there have been instances where certain drugs were prescribed for COVID -19, but clinical 
trials gave unfavorable results. The  Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends the 
Ministry to issue strict guidelines against use of such drugs when the evidence conclusively 
shows that it does not work for Covid treatment. The Committee believes that only drugs with 
reliable data and research should be used among Covid patients, especially for patients with co -
morbidities.

Management of Post-COVID Complications 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.141 The Committee understands that having defeated the virus is just the beginning of an 
unresearched path of recovery for survivors of severe COVID-19 disease, since COVID 19 is a 
new disease. The post -acute phase of SARS -CoV-2 infection depends on the severity of virus 
attack on different patients. Apart from the fear of unknown, the survivors of COVID 19 venture 
into an unchartered territory o f post COVID complications. Not only do they have to deal with 
fatigue, breathlessness and other physical effects of the disease, but also grapple with the 
psychological impact of it. The Committee is relieved to note that the Government has taken 
cognizance of complexities caused by COVID during post recovery phase and identified 
potential post-acute care needs of recovered COVID -19 patients. The Committee notes that the 
Ministry has adopted integrated holistic approach for managing patients who have recov ered 
from COVID and advised to take care at home. The Committee in this regard recommends the 
Government to put in place healthcare services to ensure a holistic follow -up of post COVID 
treatment of the patients who are showing post COVID complications. It  is also necessary to 
address the possibility of SARS -CoV- 2re-infection, the proportion of adverse reactions after 
hospital discharge and the possible development of other viral and/or bacterial infections. 
                               (Para 6.5)

Financing the Health Sector 
Observation/Recommendation 
1.180 The Committee reiterates its  considered view that the healthcare spending in India is 
abysmally low for an emerging economy with a population of 1.3 billion. Lack of desired level of 
investment in the health infrastructure has so far resulted into fragility of Indian health 
ecosystem which posed a big hurdle in generating an effective response against the pandemic. 
The Committee has time and again recommended the Ministry for increasing its spending in the 
health sector for ensuring better health infrastructure and health services to the needy common 
masses. The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the Government's reluctance to act 
upon the Committee's recommendations in letter and spirit. The Committee is assured that the 
serious impact of the pandemic could have been min imized had the Government over the years 
increased its investment in the healthcare system. The Committee is pained to note the trauma 
and distress the public had to undergo due to absence of a dedicated healthcare system. The 
Committee, therefore, strongl y recommends the Government to increase its investments in the 
public healthcare system and make consistent efforts to achieve the National Health Policy 
targets of expenditure up to 2.5% of GDP within two years as the set timeframe of year 2025 is 
far away and the public health cannot be jeopardized till that time schedule. 
                             (Para 8.10) 
1.181 The Committee is of the view that pandemic Covid -19 offers a window to revisit the 
country‟s health policy with the purpose of strengthening the health sector, and thus necessitates 
a higher investment in creating permanent basic health infrastructure. The Committee also 
believes that a higher budgetary allocation will also boost the healthcare industry and shift the 
focus to Indi an manufacturers and domestic supply chain of products. The Committee believes 
that it is the opportune time to boost India‟s healthcare infrastructure and push for greater 
technology deepening in the healthcare sector. 
                             (Para 8.12)

1.183 Ayushman Bharat, a flagship scheme of Government of India, has been launched to 
achieve the vision of Universal Health Coverage (UHC). This initiative has been designed to 
meet Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and its underlining commitment, which is to 
"leave no one behind." This scheme aims to undertake interventions to holistically address the 
healthcare system (covering prevention, promotion and ambulatory care) at the primary, 
secondary and tertiary level. Ayus hman Bharat adopts a continuum of care approach, 
comprising of two inter-related components, which are - 
 Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) 
 Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) 
1.184 Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) component envisages creation of 1 ,50,000 Health

healthcare closer to the homes of people to deliver an expanded range of services to address the 
primary health care needs of the entire population in t heir area, expanding access, universality

1.185 Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya  Yojana (PM-JAY)Ayushman Bharat PM -JAY is the largest

vulnerable families (approximately 50 crore beneficiaries) that form the bottom 40% of the 
Indian population. Since its launch in September 2018, as on 14 th April, 2021, 1,81,33,191 
hospital admission have taken place.

Observation/Recommendation 
2.8 The Committee however differs from the viewpoint of the Ministry as it feels that all the 
steps taken to contain control and minimize the incidence may appropriately be called the 
Mitigation Plan. 
                                     (Para 2.17) 
Action Taken 
2.9 The definition of „Mitigation‟, as per Disaster Management Act, 2005, includes measures 
aimed at reducing the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation. 
However specific to COVID-19 the containment plan intends to break the cycle of transmission, 
whereas a mitigation plan, intends to protect the at-risk population and Vulnerable populations to 
reduce the morbidity and mortality on such populations. Conceptually the two approaches are 
different and hence Ministry of Health & FW continues with its containment plans to 
break/suppress the chain of transmission.

better implementation of the advisories. Particularly the separate guidelines on the quarantine 
issue by different State Governments created more panic and confusion.

2.23 The clinical trials of New Drugs including COVID -19 vaccines have to be carried out as
